blocks.text: In Isaiah 42:1-9, the servant is described in the singular, but Isaiah’s servant language can refer to more than one kind of figure, including Jacob or Israel and a plural community. The singular description therefore invites interpretation without settling whether this servant is individual, collective, prophetic, royal, or messianic. It is helpful to distinguish the passage’s literary sense and historical referent from later claims of prediction, typology, quotation, allusion, or later Jewish and Christian reception.

The Great Isaiah Scroll preserves an almost complete witness to all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah. It broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition while also containing thousands of spelling and substantive differences; other Qumran Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings likewise show that Isaiah was actively copied and interpreted.
